messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi's eyes scanned the hospital ward with a mix of focus and wariness, his gaze darting between patients and staff. It had been two years since he returned from combat, but the memories still lingered, refusing to be extinguished. As a young doctor, Kofi had thought he was prepared for the worst, but nothing could have readied him for the sights and sounds of war. It started with the silence. Sudden, complete silence. It would descend upon him like a shroud, transporting him back to the desert landscape where his unit had been ambushed. The stillness would be shattered only by the sound of his own ragged breathing, as if he was reliving the moment when he thought he might suffocate under the weight of his body armor. Kofi's mind would reel, and he'd feel himself becoming detached, observing his own panic from afar. He had come to believe that this breathlessness was a harbinger of danger, a warning that he needed to be on high alert. As he navigated the hospital corridors, Kofi found himself recoiling from the sounds of violence – the raised voices, the crash of equipment, the anguished cries. His mind would snap back to the moments when his unit had come under fire, and the memories would surface in fragmented pieces: a glimpse of a comrade's terrified face, the acrid smell of smoke, the sensation of his heart racing like a jackrabbit. But there were gaps, too – parts of the event that Kofi simply couldn't recall, no matter how hard he tried to fill them in. These memory gaps only served to fuel Kofi's growing sense of unease. He felt like he was living on borrowed time, waiting for the other shoe to drop. His beliefs about the world had been shattered; he no longer trusted that things would work out for the best. Instead, he was hypervigilant, always scanning his surroundings for potential threats. Kofi's colleagues had begun to notice the change in him – the way he'd jump at sudden noises, the way his eyes seemed to bore into patients as if searching for hidden dangers. As Kofi struggled to make sense of his memories, he found himself pushing them away before they could fully surface. It was as if he was trying to protect himself from the truth, but this avoidance only served to reinforce his negative appraisals. He felt lost and disconnected from his own identity – a doctor who couldn't save everyone, a soldier who couldn't keep his comrades safe. The memories haunted him still, but it was the silence that really scared him – the silence that seemed to whisper that he'd never be able to escape the past. Kofi's avoidance behaviors had begun to take a toll on his relationships with colleagues and patients alike. He'd become withdrawn, hesitant to engage in conversations or share his expertise. His supervisors had started to notice the change, too, and Kofi knew it was only a matter of time before he faced consequences. It was this fear – the fear of losing everything he'd worked for – that finally brought him to seek help. As Kofi sat in the therapist's office, he felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he could learn to navigate these triggers and memories without becoming overwhelmed. Maybe he could rediscover the person he used to be – the person who wasn't defined by his past traumas. But for now, the silence still lingered, waiting to pounce and drag him back into the depths of his own private hell.
